summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

primary_citations.citation_text: Maryland - Md. Code, Family Law Article §§ 5-701 et seq. (Child Abuse and Neglect; definitions at § 5-701, mandatory reporting at §§ 5-704 and 5-705, investigation at § 5-706, appeal of findings at § 5-706.1)
Maryland - Courts & Judicial Proc. § 3-801 et seq. (CINA—Child in Need of Assistance proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Horridge v. St. Mary's County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: Reversing dismissal of a wrongful-death complaint, the Court held that FL § 5-706 and its regulations create a mandatory duty owed to the identified child named in an abuse report, so the public duty doctrine does not bar a negligence action against the department and its caseworkers.
key_cases.relevance: The case arose from a child beaten to death eight days after the last ignored report and defines agency liability for that outcome.
key_cases.quote: This is not an obligation that runs to everyone in general and no one in particular. It runs to an identified or identifiable child or discrete group of children.

key_cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
key_cases.holding: In a suit by an abused child against the State and social workers, the court affirmed dismissal, holding that state personnel retained statutory immunity absent malice or gross negligence, that the tort claim failed for lack of the required notice, and that violation of state-mandated investigative procedures is not itself a federal due process deprivation.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Maryland decision on remedies for serious injury suffered after the agency failed to act on abuse reports.
key_cases.quote: The violation of State-mandated procedures may well give rise to an action under State law, if the appropriate preconditions to such an action are followed

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a state agency's failure to protect a child from a known risk of parental abuse, where the child remained in his father's custody, did not deprive him of liberty in violation of the Due Process Clause.
key_cases.relevance: DeShaney is the reason that fatality and serious-injury claims against Maryland agencies proceed in state tort law rather than under § 1983.
key_cases.quote: The Clause is phrased as a limitation on the State's power to act, not as a guarantee of certain minimal levels of safety and security.

key_cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
key_cases.holding: The court vacated orders removing reunification from the permanency plan because the juvenile court relied on a polygraph examination, holding that material the department may lawfully use as an investigative tool is not thereby admissible as evidence in an adjudicative proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses proof problems where a child suffers serious injury and the perpetrator cannot be identified.
key_cases.quote: we must maintain the careful distinction between an investigative tool and evidence that has sufficient reliability for consideration in an adjudicative proceeding

extended_foster_care_age: Up to the 21st birthday, and only while the young person meets one of five conditions: completing secondary education or a program leading to an equivalent credential; enrolled in an institution providing post-secondary or vocational education; participating in a program or activity designed to promote or remove barriers to employment; employed at least 80 hours per month; or incapable of any of those due to a medical condition documented in the case plan (COMAR 07.02.11.04B). Not eligible for out-of-home placement if married, in the military, or not complying with those conditions (COMAR 07.02.11.04C). Re-entry: the juvenile court has jurisdiction over a former CINA whose commitment to the local department was rescinded after age 18 but before age 20 years 6 months and who did not exit foster care due to reunification, adoption, guardianship, marriage, or uniformed services duty, and that jurisdiction continues until age 21 (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-804(b)(2) and (c)).
